Use when you prefer a declarative component over useClusterer but still render your own map. Import from /clusterer: import { Clusterer } from 'react-native-better-clustering/clusterer' import { isClusterFeature } from 'react-native-better-clustering/geojson'

Maps visible clustered features to React elements via renderItem. <Clusterer data={geoJsonPoints} region={region} mapDimensions={{ width: mapWidth, height: mapHeight }} options={{ radius: 40, minPoints: 2, maxZoom: 20 }} renderItem={(feature) => ( <MyMarker key={ isClusterFeature(feature) ? `cluster-${feature.properties.cluster_id}` : `point-${feature.properties.id}` } feature={feature} /> )} /> Prop Type Description data PointFeature[] Points to cluster (memoize with useMemo; the index rebuilds only when coordinates change) region MapRegion Current map region mapDimensions { width, height } Map size in pixels options SuperclusterOptions Optional clustering options renderItem (feature) => ReactElement Render each visible point or cluster onError (error) => void Called when the native index fails to build; without it the error is thrown during render (see useClusterer) Thin adapter over useClusterer, with the same lifecycle, defaults, and performance notes apply. For full control, use the hook directly.

Use the low-level C++ ClusterEngine when you own map rendering and only need cluster computation, for example a custom map SDK or server-side viewport queries in a native module. Import from /engine: import { createClusterEngine, bboxToViewport, DEFAULT_SUPERCLUSTER_OPTIONS, } from 'react-native-better-clustering/engine' import { packPoints } from 'react-native-better-clustering/utils' For GeoJSON input and supercluster-compatible helpers, prefer Supercluster (used internally by useClusterer). Reach for createClusterEngine() only when you need direct buffer control. createClusterEngine(), Supercluster.load() and Supercluster.loadAsync() throw if the native module is missing from the app binary; the error says how to rebuild (see Troubleshooting).

A GeoJSON wrapper around the engine, with the query methods of supercluster. MapView hands it to superClusterRef, and useClusterer returns it. import { Supercluster } from 'react-native-better-clustering/engine' const index = new Supercluster({ radius: 40, maxZoom: 16 }) await index.loadAsync(points) // GeoJSON point features const clusters = index.getClusters([-180, -85, 180, 85], 2) index.destroy() Member Description new Supercluster(options?) Takes SuperclusterOptions, read once load(points) Builds the index on the JS thread. Once per instance loadAsync(points) Builds the index on a background thread and resolves to the instance. Once per instance isLoaded Whether the index has finished building and the instance is not destroyed getClusters(bbox, zoom) Points and clusters in a [west, south, east, north] bbox at a zoom, as in supercluster; above maxZoom, every point on its own (see Above maxZoom) getClustersFromRegion(region, mapDimensions) The same for a map region and its size in points, at the zoom picked with viewportTileSize. [] until loaded getChildren(clusterId) A cluster's direct children getLeaves(clusterId, limit = 10, offset = 0) A cluster's points, paginated. A limit of Infinity or 0 returns all getAllLeaves(clusterId, offset = 0) Every point in a cluster getClusterExpansionZoom(clusterId) The zoom at which a cluster splits into its children getClusterBounds(clusterId) The [west, south, east, north] bbox of a cluster's points, without reading them getClusterExpansionRegion(clusterId) A map region that fits a cluster's points destroy() Frees the native index. Safe to call twice; later queries throw Cluster features also carry properties.getExpansionRegion(). The query methods other than getClustersFromRegion throw until the index has loaded, and every query throws after destroy(). Unlike supercluster, there is no getTile, and load or loadAsync can be called only once per instance: create a new one for new points.

Call methods in this order: setOptions: radius, zoom range, reducers, tile extent, etc. setPoints: binary buffer from packPoints() (/utils export; must match options). build() or buildAsync(): build the spatial index. Query: getClusters, getChildren, getLeaves, getClusterBounds, getClusterExpansionZoom. dispose(): free the native index when you are done (see Native memory). setOptions or setPoints clears the index. After either call, isBuilt is false until you run build() again. const engine = createClusterEngine() engine.setOptions({ radius: 40, minPoints: 2, minZoom: 1, maxZoom: 20, extent: 512, nodeSize: 64, reducers: [], }) const { buffer } = packPoints([ { latitude: 52.23, longitude: 21.01 }, { latitude: 52.24, longitude: 21.02 }, ]) engine.setPoints(buffer) if (!engine.isBuilt) { await engine.buildAsync() // or engine.build() for small datasets } const viewport = bboxToViewport([-180, -90, 180, 90], 10) const clusters = engine.getClusters(viewport) getClusters reads the viewport as supercluster reads a bbox: across the antimeridian, pass the longitudes unwrapped (west: 170, east: 190) or wrapped (west: 170, east: -170); a span of 360° or more returns the whole world, with each feature once. getClusterExpansionZoom(id) returns the first zoom at which the cluster has split into its children, whichever zoom you saw it at, so "zoom to the expansion zoom on press" always reveals the children. It returns maxZoom + 1 for a cluster still there at maxZoom (points at the same coordinate, for example) and for a point id. getClusterBounds(id) returns the box { north, south, east, west } that every leaf under the cluster spans, without the leaves: four numbers cross into JS for a cluster of 100k points, where getLeaves would convert each point. Fit the map to it on a cluster press. A point id spans its own point. The box uses the coordinates the engine indexed, which clamps latitudes beyond ±85.05° and longitudes beyond ±180°. Supercluster has the same method, returning a [west, south, east, north] bbox, and uses it for a cluster's getExpansionRegion(). Always guard queries with isBuilt when options or points can change between renders: function queryClusters(engine: ClusterEngine, viewport: Viewport) { if (!engine.isBuilt) { return [] } return engine.getClusters(viewport) }

As in supercluster, getClusters floors the zoom and clamps it to minZoom through maxZoom + 1. At maxZoom + 1 and above it returns every point inside the viewport on its own, so points too close to split at maxZoom still come apart at street level, without raising maxZoom (which costs build time and memory). Points at the same coordinate come back as separate points on top of each other. Supercluster.getClustersFromRegion and useClusterer pick a zoom up to maxZoom + 1 too, as react-native-clusterer does; the bundled MapView stops at maxZoom and spreads such clusters out instead.

buildAsync() builds on a background thread from the points and options the engine has when you call it. Every method stays safe to call while a build is pending: Queries read one complete index each. While a build is pending they answer from the current index, or throw if isBuilt is false; they never see a half-built one. setPoints and setOptions apply to the next build. They clear isBuilt as usual, and the pending build's index is discarded when it finishes: its promise still resolves, but isBuilt stays false until you build again. Overlapping builds (buildAsync() twice, or build() while buildAsync() is pending) each settle on their own. The first to finish publishes the index; a later one of the same points and options is dropped. dispose(), or dropping the last reference to the engine, is safe mid-build: the pending build frees its index when it finishes (see Native memory). const pending = engine.buildAsync() engine.setPoints(nextBuffer) // the pending build is now stale await pending engine.isBuilt // false: build again for nextBuffer

The index lives in native memory, which grows with the number of points (the core benchmark puts 100k points spread over the world at about 43 MB). The JS garbage collector does not see that memory, so an engine you drop is freed only when the collector happens to run, and engines discarded on every data refresh can pile up. Call dispose() when you are done with an engine. It frees the index right away; if a buildAsync() is still running, the index is freed as soon as that build finishes. Any later call on the engine throws, including a second dispose(). The garbage collector learns an engine's native size only when the engine is handed to JS, which happens while it is still empty. After a build resolves, report the real size so the collector counts it: import { NitroModules } from 'react-native-nitro-modules' await engine.buildAsync() NitroModules.updateMemorySize(engine) Call it after the build resolves, not while one is pending. Supercluster, useClusterer and MapView do both for you: Supercluster.destroy() disposes its engine.

Direct ClusterEngine callers get explicit failures instead of silent empty results: Call Condition Result setOptions an option outside its valid values throws, naming the option; the previous options and index stay setPoints null / wrong layout throws getClusters, getChildren, getLeaves, getClusterBounds, getClusterExpansionZoom isBuilt === false throws getChildren, getLeaves, getClusterBounds, getClusterExpansionZoom clusterId is not a 32-bit integer (NaN, Infinity, 1.5) throws getLeaves fractional limit or offset, or NaN offset throws any method or property after dispose() throws Invalid buffers, invalid numbers and missing build() throw with messages prefixed ClusterEngine:. Use packPoints() for buffers and check isBuilt after reloads. getLeaves reads a limit of 0, a negative number, Infinity or NaN as no limit, so supercluster's getLeaves(id, Infinity) returns every leaf. A negative offset skips none. For an id that is a whole number but no node, such as -1, getChildren and getLeaves return [] and getClusterBounds returns undefined.
See Types: Headless engine for ClusterEngine, ClusterEngineOptions, Viewport, EngineClusterNode and ClusterBounds.

Use these when you render your own react-native-maps MapView and only need cluster computation, not the bundled clustered MapView. Import from /hooks: import { useClusterer } from 'react-native-better-clustering/hooks'

Computes clusters for the current viewport using the C++ engine. Returns: [features, supercluster] where features is an array of GeoJSON point or cluster features to render as markers. const [clusters, supercluster] = useClusterer( geoJsonPoints, { width: mapWidth, height: mapHeight }, region, { radius: 40, minPoints: 2, maxZoom: 20 } ) Argument Type Description data PointFeature[] GeoJSON points (memoize with useMemo) mapDimensions { width, height } Map view size in pixels region MapRegion Current map region options UseClustererOptions radius, minZoom, maxZoom, minPoints, extent, nodeSize, clusterProperties, viewportTileSize, onError Cluster features include properties.getExpansionRegion() for zoom-on-tap. Zoomed in past maxZoom, the hook returns every point on its own, as react-native-clusterer does (see Above maxZoom): markers at the same coordinate then sit on top of each other. The bundled MapView keeps them clustered and spreads them out instead. The hook destroys the underlying Supercluster engine on unmount, which frees its native index right away instead of at the next garbage collection. The index builds on a background thread via loadAsync(); comparing the points with the previous ones and packing them for the engine still run on the JS thread (see Performance model). Clusters stay empty until the first build has loaded; check supercluster.isLoaded before calling query methods directly. The index is rebuilt only when the points' coordinates, their order, or a clusterProperties source value changes: A new data array with the same content keeps the index and the returned features array. Leaf queries (getLeaves, getChildren) return the newest feature objects, so changed properties show up there without a rebuild. Point features already in features keep their identity until the region changes. When the content does change, the hook keeps returning the previous clusters while the new index builds, then swaps to the new engine and destroys the old one. A supercluster reference you hold goes stale after that swap; use the one the hook returns. One build runs at a time, and every build rebuilds the whole index. When data changes again during a build, the hook swaps to that build once it loads and then builds the newest data, skipping the arrays in between. Data that changes faster than a build loads, such as a live feed of moving markers, therefore updates the clusters once per build. If a build fails (most often because the native module is missing from the app binary, or because an option is outside its valid values), the hook throws the error during render, so the nearest error boundary (and LogBox in development) shows it. Pass onError to handle it yourself instead: the hook then keeps returning the clusters from the last successful build ([] before the first). A build that fails after newer data has arrived, or after unmount, is never reported. const [clusters] = useClusterer(geoJsonPoints, dimensions, region, { radius: 40, onError: (error) => reportToCrashlytics(error), }) Memoize data: build GeoJSON features with coordsToGeoJSONFeature inside useMemo. Inline arrays no longer rebuild the C++ index, but each render still compares every point against the previous array.

Helper to keep cluster identity stable across region updates, reducing flicker when rendering markers yourself: import { stabilizeClusterFeatures } from 'react-native-better-clustering/hooks' const stable = stabilizeClusterFeatures(previous, next) It matches a point across snapshots by its id (on properties or the feature) and its coordinates, so give an id to points that can share a coordinate: without one, two such points match the same prior feature. To match on a key of your own, pass it as the third argument. It must be unique within each array, and a feature whose key matches gets the previous object back, so include whatever must refresh it, such as its coordinates: import { isClusterFeature } from 'react-native-better-clustering/geojson' stabilizeClusterFeatures(previous, next, (feature) => { const [longitude, latitude] = feature.geometry.coordinates return isClusterFeature(feature) ? `c:${feature.properties.cluster_id}:${feature.properties.point_count}:${latitude}:${longitude}` : `p:${feature.properties.uuid}:${latitude}:${longitude}` }) useClusterer and MapView already tell co-located points apart, with or without an id. For most apps, the main MapView handles this automatically. Prefer Clusterer when you want a declarative renderItem API instead of calling the hook directly.

The main export: a clustered MapView with the same API as react-native-map-clustering. import MapView from 'react-native-better-clustering' import { Marker } from 'react-native-maps' react-native-better-clustering/compat is a backwards-compatible alias of the same component.

<MapView style={{ flex: 1 }} initialRegion={{ latitude: 52.23, longitude: 21.01, latitudeDelta: 0.35, longitudeDelta: 0.35, }} radius={56} minPoints={2} clusterColor="#FFCC00" clusterTextColor="#000000" > {points.map((point) => ( <Marker key={point.id} coordinate={{ latitude: point.latitude, longitude: point.longitude, }} /> ))} </MapView> MapView reads its marker children again whenever they change. It reuses what it made from a marker element while three things stay the same: its props object, its key, and its position among the children. When only some markers change, create the elements of the others once (for example with useMemo): a .map() in render gives every marker new props, so each one is read again. Put such a group before any list that changes length, since a list that grows or shrinks ahead of it moves its markers to new positions.

All standard react-native-maps MapView props are supported, plus: Prop Default Description radius ~6% of screen width Cluster radius in pixels. The default matches react-native-map-clustering and is smaller than the default bubble; for dense data pass about twice it (around 50 on a phone), see Troubleshooting minPoints 2 Minimum points to form a cluster minZoom 1 Minimum zoom level maxZoom 20 Maximum zoom level for clustering extent 512 Tile extent, in supercluster's sense: radius is in pixels of an extent-wide tile, so a larger extent clusters more tightly at the same radius nodeSize 64 KD-tree leaf size clusteringEnabled true Toggle clustering spiralEnabled true Spread markers that share a location (a cluster that zooming can't split) into a spiral with connector lines. See Markers at the same location spiderfyMinZoom 19 Camera zoom from which such clusters spread without being pressed (react-native-map-clustering parity) spiderfyMaxLeaves 50 Most markers a cluster spiderfies into. A larger cluster of overlapping markers stays a bubble; pressing it still calls onClusterPress with every marker, so you can list them instead. Spider markers are spaced about 40 pt apart on screen spiderLineColor #FF0000 Color of spider connector lines clusterColor #0F52FF Default cluster bubble color (GMI brand blue) clusterTextColor #FFFFFF Default cluster label color clusterFontFamily None Font family for the cluster count label; also passed to renderCluster clusterAccessibilityLabel (count) => `Cluster of ${count} markers` Accessibility label for a default cluster bubble, passed to its Marker with the button role. Screen readers do not announce it yet: see Accessibility animationEnabled true Fade and glide the default cluster bubbles on zoom (iOS + Android); see clusterFadeInDuration layoutAnimationConf None Deprecated and ignored, accepted for react-native-map-clustering compatibility. LayoutAnimation cannot animate map markers on the New Architecture: they are native map annotations outside React Native's layout. Tune the fade with clusterFadeInDuration clusterFadeInDuration 250 Cross-fade duration (ms) for default cluster bubbles on zoom: new bubbles fade in while removed ones linger and fade out, eliminating the blink from native annotations being added/removed (iOS + Android). Driven by Reanimated on the UI thread; without the optional react-native-reanimated peer, bubbles do not fade and removed ones disappear at once. Bubbles cross-fade when the map settles; during an active pinch/pan, new bubbles appear at once and removed ones stay for up to 100 ms (never longer than this duration) before they go, so a continuous zoom leaves no gaps; at the default clusterUpdateIntervalMs at most one extra generation of bubbles stays mounted. It also times the glide: on a zoom step, a splitting cluster's new bubbles start at its place and glide to theirs, a bubble whose cluster moves slides there, and merging bubbles glide into the one that takes them in (while the map moves, within the 100 ms they stay); pans and data changes only fade. Gated by animationEnabled; ignored with a custom renderCluster. Set to 0 to disable tracksViewChanges false Forwarded to default cluster markers edgePadding 50px each side Padding for fitToCoordinates on cluster press preserveClusterPressBehavior false Skip auto fitToCoordinates on cluster press selectedClusterId None Highlight a cluster by id selectedClusterColor #FF5722 Color when cluster is selected width / height window size Seed map dimensions before onLayout clusterUpdateIntervalMs 100 Minimum interval (ms) between cluster recomputations while the map is moving; 0 recomputes only on settle clusterRenderMargin 100 How far outside the map, in points, cluster bubbles still render. Clusters are found, and reported to onMarkersChange, for the region plus half its size on each side, as in react-native-map-clustering; only rendering stops at this margin, and markers are not affected. A smaller margin mounts fewer native annotations on each zoom step, which keeps the UI thread free for the bubble fade; a larger one leaves fewer bubbles to appear at the edges during a fast pan. Infinity renders every cluster found superClusterRef None Receives the loaded Supercluster behind the clusters on screen, or null. It is replaced after each rebuild and the previous engine destroyed, so read current when you query instead of keeping it; see superClusterRef mapRef None Callback ref to the inner react-native-maps instance style applies to a View that wraps the map, and the map fills that view. radius, minPoints, minZoom, maxZoom, extent and nodeSize must be in their valid ranges. An invalid one fails like a failed build (passed to onError, or thrown during render without it), with a message that names the prop.

Prop Signature Description onClusterPress (cluster, markers) => void Fired when a cluster is tapped, with every marker in it. The markers are read only when you pass this prop; for a cluster of tens of thousands that read is most of what a press costs. The map fits the cluster's bounds either way onMarkersChange (markers) => void Fired when visible markers/clusters change: once the first index has loaded, then only when the visible set changes. A re-render with the same marker coordinates does not fire it, so onMarkersChange={setState} is safe onRegionChangeComplete (region, details, markers) => void Extends the maps callback with current markers, in react-native-map-clustering 4.x's order. 3.x passed (region, markers): see Coming from react-native-map-clustering 3.x onError (error) => void Fired when the native cluster index fails to build, for example because the app was not rebuilt after installing the library. Markers from an earlier successful build keep showing. Without it, the error is thrown during render so an error boundary (and LogBox in development) shows it. See Troubleshooting

Markers at the same coordinate (one building, or geocoding fallbacks) form a cluster that zooming can never split. With spiralEnabled, MapView spreads them into a spiral: automatically from camera zoom spiderfyMinZoom (19 by default), and at any zoom when the cluster is pressed. The map doesn't move; the spiral collapses when the zoom changes. This also covers maps whose maximum zoom (maxZoomLevel, or the provider's limit) sits below spiderfyMinZoom. onClusterPress still receives the cluster and its markers. Clusters of distinct nearby markers keep expanding by zooming, and clusters larger than spiderfyMaxLeaves stay bubbles. With preserveClusterPressBehavior, a press only calls onClusterPress. MapView never clusters at a zoom above maxZoom, so a cluster still there at maxZoom stays a cluster however far the map zooms in, and spreads out as above. useClusterer instead returns its markers on their own there (see Above maxZoom).
When the map spans ±180°, the markers on both sides show. As in supercluster, markers on opposite sides never join one cluster.

MapView clusters a child when it is an element with its own coordinate prop and without cluster={false}, as react-native-map-clustering does. Arrays are flattened, so several {items.map(…)} lists can sit side by side. Every other child renders as it is, unclustered, and so does each marker inside it: <MapView> {/* Clustered: each child is an element with a `coordinate` prop. */} {shops.map((shop) => ( <Marker key={shop.id} coordinate={shop.location} /> ))} {cafes.map((cafe) => ( <CafeMarker key={cafe.id} coordinate={cafe.location} cafe={cafe} /> ))} {/* Not clustered: neither the Fragment nor `<ParkPin>` has a `coordinate` prop. */} <> {stations.map((station) => ( <Marker key={station.id} coordinate={station.location} /> ))} </> {parks.map((park) => ( <ParkPin key={park.id} park={park} /> ))} </MapView> A component such as CafeMarker is clustered by its coordinate prop and renders as itself when it stands alone, so it must render a Marker at that coordinate. Spiderfy passes it a new coordinate. Give every marker a stable key (see Markers flicker on zoom).

Markers cluster by default (cluster omitted or cluster={true}). Exclude individual markers from clustering: <Marker cluster={false} coordinate={{ latitude: 52.23, longitude: 21.01 }} /> react-native-maps does not declare cluster, so importing from react-native-better-clustering (or /compat) adds it to the props TypeScript checks on Marker. It cannot add it to MapMarkerProps, a type alias, so MapMarkerProps, React.ComponentProps<typeof Marker> and MarkerAnimated go without it. Type a component that takes cluster and passes it on to a Marker with MapMarkerProps & { cluster?: boolean }.

Moving, adding or removing a clustered marker rebuilds the whole native index on a background thread; the index is never patched. The map keeps showing the previous markers until the new index has loaded. Builds run one at a time: markers that change during a build are built once it has loaded, from the newest children, so markers that move faster than a build loads update on the map once per build. Any change to the children, even to a marker that does not cluster, costs a pass over the markers on the JS thread: MapView reads them and compares them with the previous children to tell whether the index needs rebuilding. A rebuild then also packs every clustered marker for the native build, whose time grows with their number. To keep live updates cheap: Create the elements of markers that do not move once (with useMemo), so only the moving markers are new elements on each update. Give moving markers that do not need to cluster cluster={false}. They skip the index, so moving them never rebuilds it. The example app's Live fleet scenario measures both, with up to 50,000 static markers and vehicles that move up to 10 times a second.

Pass renderCluster for full control over the cluster bubble: import MapView, { type RenderClusterProps, } from 'react-native-better-clustering' import { Marker } from 'react-native-maps' const renderCluster = (cluster: RenderClusterProps) => { const [longitude, latitude] = cluster.geometry.coordinates return ( <Marker coordinate={{ latitude, longitude }} onPress={cluster.onPress} tracksViewChanges={cluster.tracksViewChanges} > {/* your cluster bubble */} </Marker> ) } <MapView renderCluster={renderCluster} {...props}> {/* markers */} </MapView> Cluster features include properties.point_count, properties.point_count_abbreviated, and properties.getExpansionRegion() for zoom-on-tap.

Each default cluster bubble passes an accessibilityLabel and the button role to its Marker. The label is Cluster of N markers, or what clusterAccessibilityLabel returns for the number of markers: <MapView clusterAccessibilityLabel={(count) => t('map.cluster', { count })} {...props} > {/* markers */} </MapView> Screen readers do not announce it yet. react-native-maps (up to 1.29) does not pass a Marker's accessibilityLabel or accessibilityRole to the native map annotation: on iOS with Apple Maps, VoiceOver reads a cluster bubble as "Map pin", and on Android the label does not reach the Google Maps marker. A renderCluster marker has the same limit. The bubbles announce their label once react-native-maps passes it on; follow react-native-maps#6046.
import type { ClusteredMapViewProps, RenderClusterProps, } from 'react-native-better-clustering' ClusteredMapViewProps is the full props type for the clustered MapView.

import type { ClusteredMapViewProps, RenderClusterProps, } from 'react-native-better-clustering' ClusteredMapViewProps extends react-native-maps MapViewProps with clustering options (radius, minPoints, onClusterPress, renderCluster, etc.). RenderClusterProps is passed to renderCluster: a ClusterFeature plus onPress, clusterColor, clusterTextColor, clusterFontFamily, and tracksViewChanges.

import type { PointFeature, ClusterFeature, PointOrClusterFeature, BBox, } from 'react-native-better-clustering/geojson' Cluster properties include cluster, cluster_id, point_count, point_count_abbreviated, and getExpansionRegion().
import type { SuperclusterOptions, ClusterPropertyConfig, MapDimensions, } from 'react-native-better-clustering/engine'

Option Default Description radius 40 Cluster radius in pixels minZoom 1 Min zoom for clustering maxZoom 20 Max zoom for clustering. Queries above it return every point on its own (see Above maxZoom) minPoints 2 Min points to form a cluster extent 512 Tile extent used for projection math (see note) nodeSize 64 KD-tree leaf size clusterProperties [] Numeric point properties to aggregate into each cluster: { source, key?, reduce }, where reduce is 'sum', 'min' or 'max'. supercluster's map and reduce functions are not supported viewportTileSize extent Tile size used to pick a zoom from a map region (see note) Valid values​ Loading points throws a RangeError naming the first option outside these ranges, instead of building an empty or unbounded index: Option Must be radius A finite number >= 0 minZoom, maxZoom Integers from 0 to 30 (supercluster's limit), with minZoom <= maxZoom extent An integer >= 1 minPoints, nodeSize 32-bit integers. Below 2 and 1 they act as 2 and 1 viewportTileSize A finite number > 0 useClusterer, Clusterer and MapView pass the error to onError, or throw it during render when onError is not set. Radius and extent​ radius and extent mean exactly what they mean in supercluster: radius is the cluster radius in pixels of a tile that is extent pixels wide, so the two are read together as radius / extent. Raising extent therefore tightens clustering and lowering it loosens clustering, at the same radius. Given the same options and zoom, this package produces the same clusters as supercluster, apart from two edge cases (points exactly on the radius boundary, and tie-breaking with minPoints above 2) described under supercluster parity. Viewport tile size​ viewportTileSize is separate from extent. It only affects getClustersFromRegion (how a map region plus a pixel size is turned into a zoom level) and shifts the result by a whole zoom level: Value Parity with 256 react-native-map-clustering (geo-viewport's default). Correct for map dimensions in logical points, which is what onLayout reports. 512 (= extent, the default) react-native-clusterer, which passes its extent to geo-viewport. One zoom level lower. The MapView compat layer sets 256 so a drop-in swap renders the same clusters. useClusterer and Supercluster default to extent, keeping react-native-clusterer parity; pass viewportTileSize: 256 to opt in.

Low-level Nitro hybrid object; create it via createClusterEngine() from /engine. See the headless engine guide for lifecycle, isBuilt checks, and error behavior. import { createClusterEngine, type ClusterBounds, type ClusterEngine, type ClusterEngineOptions, type EngineClusterNode, type Viewport, } from 'react-native-better-clustering/engine' Each EngineClusterNode has minLeafId: the smallest point id among its leaves (its own id for a point). A cluster keeps it across zoom levels while it only gains or loses other leaves, so it can key the cluster's marker. Lifecycle: setOptions → setPoints (packPoints() buffer) → build() → query. Query methods throw when isBuilt is false; setPoints throws on invalid buffers.
Requirement Supported React Native 0.78+ (New Architecture required) Map rendering react-native-maps Expo Development build (not Expo Go)

Package Version Required react-native-maps >=1.20.1 Yes react-native-nitro-modules >=0.32.0 Yes (declared optional, see below) react-native-reanimated ^4.1.0 No: only animates the default cluster bubbles react-native-maps: 1.20.1 is the version Expo SDK 54 installs. It runs on the New Architecture through React Native's interop layer; 1.21.0 is the first release with native Fabric components. react-native-nitro-modules: the generated bindings need 0.32.0 or newer and fail to compile against older versions. The package declares it as an optional * peer, as Nitro recommends for libraries, so the app chooses the Nitro version and a pre-release Nitro never gets a second, stable copy installed next to it. Install it yourself. react-native-reanimated: when it is missing, cluster bubbles render without the fade or glide. react-native-worklets is Reanimated's own dependency, not this library's; install the version your Reanimated asks for.
Change one import; the props and <Marker> children carry over. See Migrating from react-native-map-clustering for the differences, and for onRegionChangeComplete when you come from 3.x.

For custom map stacks, use advanced subpaths: react-native-clusterer This package useClusterer /hooks Supercluster /engine isClusterFeature /geojson The default zoom range differs: minZoom is 1 and maxZoom is 20 here, where react-native-clusterer uses supercluster's 0 and 16. Pass both to keep the clusters you had. Extra: clusterProperties aggregates a numeric point property into each cluster with sum, min or max (see SuperclusterOptions). supercluster's map and reduce functions are not supported.

The C++ engine reproduces supercluster's algorithm feature-for-feature. Checked-in fixtures in package/cpp/ClusterEngineCore.test.cpp, generated from supercluster 8.0.1 and verified in CI, pin it: Six seeded cases of 3,000–8,000 points spread over the world (extent 256, 512 and 1024, minPoints: 2): at every zoom from minZoom to maxZoom + 1, where every point stands on its own, the engine must return the same number of features and of clusters, group the same points into each cluster, and give each cluster the same expansion zoom. The six benchmark datasets (uniform, a city, blobs, identical points, a grid and points across the antimeridian, 5,000 points each) at every zoom from 1 to 21, with and without clusterProperties: the same checks, plus each cluster's centroid and its sum, min and max aggregates. Viewport queries around the antimeridian, with the bbox written unwrapped, wrapped, far outside ±180° and 360° or wider. Two deliberate differences remain: Precision. supercluster rounds projected coordinates to Float32 and keeps its KD-trees in a Float32Array; the C++ engine keeps them as double. Centroids are therefore slightly more accurate here (supercluster's can be off by up to about 2e-5° of longitude), and on dense data a point near the edge of the radius can fall on the other side of it, which changes which points share a cluster. On the benchmark's city dataset (5,000 points within about 50 km) that happens at 10 of 21 zooms: 64 to 131 points end up in another cluster at zooms 7 to 10, where clusters are largest, and 1 to 11 from zoom 11 up. The sparser datasets differ for one point at one zoom, or not at all. The fixtures compare against supercluster with that rounding taken out, which the engine matches exactly, and list the zooms where stock supercluster differs. Tie-breaking with minPoints above 2. Clustering is a greedy single pass, so the order in which equidistant neighbours are visited can decide which of two overlapping groups wins. The engine and supercluster walk their KD-trees in different orders. With the default minPoints: 2 this is unobservable.

Clustering parity also depends on which zoom a map region is queried at, and the two upstreams disagree by a whole zoom level. viewportTileSize selects which one you get: Entry point viewportTileSize Matches MapView (main export) 256 react-native-map-clustering useClusterer, Supercluster extent (512) react-native-clusterer useClusterer and Supercluster accept a viewportTileSize option to override their default; pass 256 to query the same zoom as MapView. MapView has no such prop and always uses 256, as react-native-map-clustering does. See SuperclusterOptions. Earlier releases normalised the cluster radius incorrectly, clustering at roughly half the requested radius on the default extent: 512, and queried MapView one zoom level below react-native-map-clustering. The two errors largely cancelled at the shipped defaults, so MapView looked about right while useClusterer did not. Both are fixed. If you tuned radius against the old /engine or /hooks behaviour, multiply it by 256 / extent to keep the previous clustering: halve it at the default extent: 512, keep it at 256, quarter it at 1024. Earlier releases also clamped every query to maxZoom, so /engine and /hooks never returned unclustered points: points closer than the cluster radius at maxZoom stayed clustered however far the map zoomed in. As in supercluster and react-native-clusterer, a query above maxZoom now returns every point on its own (see Above maxZoom). MapView is unchanged: it stops at maxZoom and spiderfies those clusters.

react-native-better-clustering is a drop-in replacement for react-native-map-clustering: same MapView + <Marker> API, with a C++ supercluster engine via Nitro Modules instead of supercluster in JavaScript.
- import MapView from 'react-native-map-clustering' + import MapView from 'react-native-better-clustering' See Migrating from react-native-map-clustering for the differences.

react-native-map-clustering builds its supercluster index in JavaScript, on the JS thread, so a large dataset holds up touches and renders while it loads. MapView here builds the index in C++ on a background thread instead, without changing how you write map screens. Reading the clusters for the visible region is a synchronous native call from the JS thread, and markers still render through react-native-maps.
Need full control over rendering? Use subpath exports: /hooks: useClusterer when you own the MapView /engine: Supercluster class and geometry helpers /geojson: GeoJSON conversion utilities

Quick Start: install and render your first clustered map. Platform Setup: peers and prebuild. Migrating from react-native-map-clustering: what differs. MapView API: props, callbacks, and customization. Hooks API: useClusterer for custom stacks.

The main export is the clustered MapView, with the props and callbacks of react-native-map-clustering 4.0. react-native-better-clustering/compat is a backwards-compatible alias. Change one import: - import MapView from 'react-native-map-clustering' + import MapView from 'react-native-better-clustering' Your <Marker> children, clustering props and react-native-maps props carry over. Children are picked for clustering by the same rule (see Which children are clustered). Check the differences below, and if you come from 3.x, the onRegionChangeComplete arguments. Unlike react-native-map-clustering, this package has native code: it needs React Native 0.78+ with the New Architecture, react-native-nitro-modules, and a rebuild of the app (a development build with Expo, not Expo Go). See Platform Setup.

react-native-map-clustering 4.0 This package onRegionChangeComplete (region, details, markers); 3.x passed (region, markers) (region, details, markers), called once the clusters for the settled region are computed. Development builds warn about a handler that declares two parameters (from 3.x) onMarkersChange Called each time the region settles Called once the first index has loaded, then whenever the visible markers and clusters change, also while the map moves clusterColor default #00B386 (green) #0F52FF (blue). Pass clusterColor="#00B386" to keep the old color Default cluster bubble Two circles in clusterColor, with the full count A ring and a shadow, with counts from 1,000 abbreviated (1.2k). Pass renderCluster to draw your own style Applied to the map Applied to a View that wraps the map; the map fills that view. Sizing and positioning styles behave the same, but padding now insets the map animationEnabled Runs layoutAnimationConf when the region settles, on iOS Fades and glides the default cluster bubbles on zoom, on iOS and Android, with the optional react-native-reanimated (see clusterFadeInDuration) layoutAnimationConf LayoutAnimation config, spring by default Accepted and ignored: LayoutAnimation cannot animate map markers on the New Architecture Spiderfy From camera zoom 19, once a cluster has been pressed From camera zoom spiderfyMinZoom (19), or at any zoom when pressed; only clusters that zooming can't split, of at most spiderfyMaxLeaves markers. See Markers at the same location Zoomed in past maxZoom With a maxZoom below 20, every marker shows on its own, and markers at one location stack Clusters stay as they are at maxZoom, and spiderfy as above Cluster press Fits the map to every marker in the cluster Fits the map to the cluster's bounds: the same region, without reading every marker unless you pass onClusterPress superClusterRef A supercluster instance, rebuilt on the JS thread whenever the children change A Supercluster on the native engine, built in the background (see below) Build failures No onError prop A failed native build, or an invalid clustering prop, is thrown during render, unless you pass onError <Marker cluster={false}> in TypeScript Does not type-check: no type declares cluster Type-checks (see Per-marker opt-out). A @ts-expect-error you added for it now fails as unused: remove it MapView also adds props react-native-map-clustering does not have, such as spiderfyMinZoom, spiderfyMaxLeaves, clusterFadeInDuration, clusterUpdateIntervalMs, clusterRenderMargin and onError. See the MapView API.

onRegionChangeComplete follows react-native-map-clustering 4.x: it receives (region, details, markers). 3.x passed (region, markers), so a handler written for 3.x now gets the details of react-native-maps where it expects the markers. TypeScript only catches this when the handler's parameters have types. Take the markers from the third argument: <MapView - onRegionChangeComplete={(region, markers) => setVisible(markers)} + onRegionChangeComplete={(region, details, markers) => setVisible(markers)} > In development, MapView warns once when the handler declares exactly two parameters (a parameter with a default value, and every one after it, does not count). A handler that means (region, details) can declare the third parameter, (region, details, _markers) => …, to silence the notice.

superClusterRef.current is a Supercluster, not a supercluster instance. It has supercluster's query methods (getClusters, getChildren, getLeaves, getClusterExpansionZoom), but no getTile, and it changes at different times: The index builds on a background thread. Until the first build has loaded, current is null, so check it before you query. When markers are added, removed, moved or reordered, the previous engine keeps serving queries until the new index has loaded. Then current is replaced and the previous engine destroyed, so read superClusterRef.current when you query instead of keeping the instance: a destroyed one throws. With clusteringEnabled={false}, and after the map unmounts, current is null. Whenever current is not null, it is loaded and ready to query.

Issue Status Crash on NaN zoom (#294) Guarded Map size can't be 0 on Android (#285) Layout-aware maxZoom / spiralEnabled ignored (#274, #275) Implemented Unstable clusters on zoom (#255) Stable references Per-marker cluster={false} (#297) Supported
The index builds asynchronously, queries are synchronous, and rendering is the ceiling. Where each step runs decides what a large dataset costs.

Step Where it runs When Turning <Marker> children into points, and comparing them with the previous points JS thread Each render with new children Packing the points into a buffer (packPoints) and copying them into the engine (setPoints) JS thread; the copy is a synchronous native call When markers are added, removed, moved or reordered Building the index A background thread After each copy Finding the clusters in the region (getClusters) JS thread, a synchronous native call Each region update; while the map moves, at most every clusterUpdateIntervalMs Reading a cluster's markers (getLeaves) JS thread, a synchronous native call On a cluster press with onClusterPress, and for spiderfy Mounting and drawing markers and cluster bubbles react-native-maps, on the UI thread Whenever the visible markers and clusters change Fading and gliding the default bubbles Reanimated, on the UI thread On zoom

Building. react-native-map-clustering builds its supercluster index on the JS thread. Here, turning the children into points, packing them and copying them into the engine run there, but the build does not. Those steps still grow with the number of markers. Querying. A query blocks the JS thread for as long as it takes, and returns only the features in the region. Rendering is the ceiling. Each visible marker and cluster is a native map annotation that react-native-maps mounts. With hundreds on screen, a zoom step that replaces them costs more than clustering. Keep the count down with a larger radius (see Zooming stutters with many markers), a smaller clusterRenderMargin, and stable keys on your markers.

The core benchmark measures the C++ engine alone on a desktop CPU: build and query times, and memory, for six datasets of up to 100k points. It says nothing about Hermes, the JS layer or rendering on a phone, so it cannot back a claim about app frame rates. The device benchmark measures the whole pipeline instead: the example app in a Release build on Hermes, rendering included, running this library and react-native-map-clustering 4.0.0 through the same script. Its first run, on the iOS Simulator, reports the time to the first markers, JS freezes, memory, zoom and cluster presses for 10k, 50k and 100k markers. A simulator runs on the Mac's CPU, faster than a phone: compare the libraries, not the absolute times.

Today this library moves clustering compute to C++. Visible markers are still rendered through react-native-maps <Marker> components, which is the ceiling described above. Near term, within react-native-maps: image-based cluster bubbles with caching, stable marker pooling and smarter defaults. Still bounded by the cost of each annotation. The goal: a native render layer. The C++ engine feeds packed point data directly into native bubble rendering, drawn in a single native pass instead of one React <Marker> per cluster or point, behind the same MapView + <Marker> API. Track progress in GitHub Issues.

React Native 0.78+ with the New Architecture enabled. react-native-nitro-modules 0.32.0 or newer (required). react-native-maps 1.20.1 or newer (required). react-native-reanimated 4.1 or a later 4.x (optional): fades and glides the cluster bubbles on zoom.

npm install react-native-better-clustering react-native-nitro-modules react-native-maps cd ios && pod install Expo requires a development build: npx expo install react-native-better-clustering react-native-nitro-modules react-native-maps See Platform Setup for react-native-maps plugin config and the optional Reanimated animation.

import MapView from 'react-native-better-clustering' import { Marker } from 'react-native-maps' const points = [ { id: '1', latitude: 52.23, longitude: 21.01 }, { id: '2', latitude: 52.24, longitude: 21.02 }, ] export function MapScreen() { return ( <MapView style={{ flex: 1 }} initialRegion={{ latitude: 52.0, longitude: 19.0, latitudeDelta: 8, longitudeDelta: 8, }} radius={50} minPoints={2} clusterColor="#0F52FF" > {points.map((point) => ( <Marker key={point.id} coordinate={{ latitude: point.latitude, longitude: point.longitude, }} /> ))} </MapView> ) }

Change one import; props and <Marker> children carry over: - import MapView from 'react-native-map-clustering' + import MapView from 'react-native-better-clustering' Coming from 3.x? onRegionChangeComplete receives (region, details, markers), as in 4.x, not (region, markers). See Migrating from react-native-map-clustering for that and the other differences.

If you render your own react-native-maps MapView and only need cluster computation, use useClusterer from /hooks: import { useMemo, useState } from 'react' import MapView, { Marker } from 'react-native-maps' import { useClusterer } from 'react-native-better-clustering/hooks' import { coordsToGeoJSONFeature, isClusterFeature, } from 'react-native-better-clustering/geojson' See Hooks API.

npm install react-native-better-clustering react-native-nitro-modules react-native-maps cd ios && pod install Peer dependency Version react-native-maps >=1.20.1 Required react-native-nitro-modules >=0.32.0 Required react-native-reanimated ^4.1.0 Optional, see Reanimated react-native-nitro-modules is declared as an optional peer dependency, as Nitro recommends for libraries, so package managers never install it on their own: the app picks the Nitro version. Install it yourself, at 0.32.0 or newer. The native build fails on older versions (see Troubleshooting).

With Reanimated installed, the default cluster bubbles cross-fade on zoom, and a splitting cluster's parts glide out of it while merging clusters glide into one, all animated on the UI thread (see clusterFadeInDuration). Install it by following Reanimated's own installation guide: it needs react-native-worklets and, in bare React Native, the Worklets Babel plugin. Without Reanimated, clusters still render: bubbles appear and disappear without a fade or glide, and development builds log a one-time notice. Pass clusterFadeInDuration={0} to opt out of the fade and the notice.
This library is a Nitro module and requires React Native's New Architecture. Confirm it is enabled and rebuild the native app.

Use a development build, not Expo Go. npx expo install react-native-better-clustering react-native-nitro-modules react-native-maps For the cluster fade, add Reanimated as well; babel-preset-expo configures its Babel plugin: npx expo install react-native-reanimated react-native-worklets Add the react-native-maps config plugin to app.json: { "expo": { "plugins": [ [ "react-native-maps", { "androidGoogleMapsApiKey": "YOUR_GOOGLE_MAPS_API_KEY" } ] ] } } The plugin reads androidGoogleMapsApiKey, not googleMapsApiKey: without it, Android apps crash with "API key not found" when a map mounts. iOS uses Apple Maps and needs no key, unless you render with provider={PROVIDER_GOOGLE}; then add iosGoogleMapsApiKey too. The plugin ships with react-native-maps 1.22.0 and newer, which Expo SDK 55 and later install. Expo SDK 53 and 54 install 1.20.1, which has no plugin, and expo prebuild stops with a PluginError saying react-native-maps has no valid config plugin. On those SDKs, leave react-native-maps out of plugins and set expo.android.config.googleMaps.apiKey instead (and expo.ios.config.googleMapsApiKey for Google Maps on iOS). Then regenerate native projects: npx expo prebuild --clean
If not using Expo, add your API key to AndroidManifest.xml: <meta-data android:name="com.google.android.geo.API_KEY" android:value="YOUR_GOOGLE_MAPS_API_KEY"/>
Configure a Google Maps API key for react-native-maps (Expo plugin or AndroidManifest.xml). Ensure the key has "Maps SDK for Android" enabled.

With Expo, pass the key to the react-native-maps plugin as androidGoogleMapsApiKey (the plugin ignores googleMapsApiKey), then run npx expo prebuild --clean. On Expo SDK 53 and 54, whose react-native-maps 1.20.1 has no plugin, set expo.android.config.googleMaps.apiKey instead. See Installation.

documents.t: This library is a Nitro module and requires React Native's New Architecture. Confirm it is enabled and rebuild the native app.

The native build stops with one or both of: react-native-better-clustering needs react-native-nitro-modules 0.32.0 or newer. Upgrade it, then reinstall pods (iOS) or rebuild (Android). NitroModules cannot be found! Are you sure you installed NitroModules properly? The library's generated Nitro bindings need react-native-nitro-modules 0.32.0 or newer. Against an older Nitro they fail with the second message even though Nitro is installed; the first one, from the library's own code, names the cause. Nitro is older than 0.32.0: upgrade it, then rebuild (cd ios && pod install in bare React Native, npx expo prebuild --clean with Expo). Nitro is not in your package.json: install it. It is a peer dependency that package managers do not install for you, so the app decides which Nitro version it runs.

With Android Gradle Plugin 9, the Android build fails with an error about the Kotlin Gradle plugin (Cannot add extension with name 'kotlin'), or about libraryVariants / applicationVariants, once an app turns on AGP 9's built-in Kotlin or its new DSL. The React Native 0.87 and 0.88 app templates and react-native-nitro-modules (0.37.1 and earlier) still apply the Kotlin plugin themselves, so keep the opt-outs those templates set in android/gradle.properties: android.builtInKotlin=false android.newDsl=false

documents.t: react-native-better-clustering: the native ClusterEngine module is not available. Rebuild the app after installing the library (`pod install` on iOS, a Gradle build on Android, or `npx expo prebuild` and a development build with Expo); Expo Go is not supported. Cause: … The JavaScript side is installed but the app binary does not contain the native engine. Rebuild the native app after installing or upgrading the library: Bare React Native: cd ios && pod install, then rebuild both platforms. Expo: npx expo prebuild --clean, then build a development build. Expo Go cannot load it. MapView, Clusterer and useClusterer throw this error during render, so an error boundary (and LogBox in development) shows it. To handle it yourself instead, pass onError; the map then renders without the clustered markers.

documents.t: Correct: native modules require a development build. Run npx expo prebuild --clean and build the app.

documents.t: You called a method on a Supercluster after destroy(). Create a new instance. useClusterer handles lifecycle automatically, but it destroys the previous engine once a rebuild for changed data has loaded: use the supercluster from the latest render rather than one kept from earlier.

The index rebuilds only when coordinates, their order, or a clusterProperties source value change. If it still rebuilds on every render, the data itself changes: for example, coordinates recomputed with floating-point noise, or a list re-sorted on each render. Memoize your GeoJSON input: const geoJson = useMemo( () => points.map((point) => coordsToGeoJSONFeature( { latitude: point.latitude, longitude: point.longitude }, { id: point.id } ) ), [points] )

Give every Marker a stable key (its id, not its array index). MapView keeps that key, so adding or removing a marker doesn't remount the others, and it keys each cluster bubble by its first marker's key, so a cluster that splits or merges on zoom, or survives a data update, keeps its native marker instead of being removed and re-added. Memoize custom marker components too. With /hooks, use stabilizeClusterFeatures and key your markers by a stable point id.

The default radius matches react-native-map-clustering, so a drop-in swap draws the same clusters. With the default extent: 512 it clusters markers that are about 12–24 pt apart on screen, while a default cluster bubble is 32–56 pt wide. Dense data therefore covers the map with overlapping bubbles, and every zoom step mounts hundreds of new native markers, which stalls the map. Pass a larger radius, about twice the default: roughly 12% of the map width, which is around 50 on a phone: <MapView radius={Dimensions.get('window').width * 0.12}>{markers}</MapView> In the example app's 50,000-marker scenario on an iOS simulator, doubling the radius cut the bubbles on screen by about two thirds and made the longest frame during a pinch about four times shorter. Each cluster then covers a larger area, so pressing one zooms in less.

Points whose latitude or longitude is not a finite number (undefined, null, or NaN) cannot be projected, so they are skipped when the index is built. This is common with data straight from an API, where a missing field turns into undefined. In development the library warns once per load with the count and the first few offending indices: react-native-better-clustering: skipped 2 of 480 points with non-finite coordinates (index 17, 291). Check those points for undefined, null, or NaN latitude/longitude: they will not appear on the map. Filter or repair those points before loading them: const usablePoints = useMemo( () => points.filter( (point) => Number.isFinite(point.latitude) && Number.isFinite(point.longitude) ), [points] ) Out-of-range values behave differently: a latitude beyond ±85.05 or a longitude beyond ±180 is clamped to the Web Mercator limits rather than skipped, so such a marker still renders, just at the edge of the projection.
